newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria to receive fresh nuclear fuel from Russia.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria to receive fresh nuclear fuel from Russia.

text.p: Bulgaria will receive fresh nuclear fuel from Russia at the end of this week for its Soviet-made power plant at Kozloduy, energy officials said on Monday.
They said the fuel would be used for recharging 1,000- megawatt reactor number six at the Kozloduy plant, which has another 1,000-megawatt reactor and four 440-megawatt reactors.
"Reactor number six will be restarted at the beginning of November as scheduled," National Electricity Co chairman Kozma Kuzmanov told Reuters.
He denied media reports that Russia had cut or suspended nuclear fuel supplies to Bulgaria.
Kuzmanov said there could be power supply difficulties in the country if Kozloduy's oldest 440-megawatt reactor number one was not put on stream in December and then power cuts would be introduced.
Kozloduy closed its oldest reactor in May to take samples from the metal of the reactor's vessel after the European Union urged its closure because of safety fears.
Preliminary results from the analysis are expected at the beginning of November and if they show the reactor is safe it will be restarted at the beginning of December, Kuzmanov said.
"We expect difficulties with power supplies if we are without reactor number one at the beginning of January," he said.
Bulgaria's overstretched energy industry was forced to ration electricity supplies between 1978 and 1993.
A sharp rise in power charges has forced some 11 percent of households to make drastic cuts in central heating this coming winter, Kuzmanov said.
"These people have applied to cut central heating in a number of rooms but not in the whole flat and we expect them to raise electricity consumption only by 30-40 megawatts," he said.
Some 1.5 million city-dwellers among Bulgaria's 8.5 million people have access to central heating.
Under Communist rule, which ended in 1989, state-subsidised fuel prices were unrealistically low and Bulgarians developed wasteful habits. Consumers used to open windows to cool overheated homes.
